Nobody puts this in the headline

Here’s the part nobody puts in the headline: the free voices don’t belong to you. Meta’s own terms keep ownership of the voices with Meta, so you’re building on borrowed ground.

I know, because I stood exactly where you’re standing. I found voices that sounded genuinely human, warm, conversational, the kind of voice that’s hard to find in AI, and I started planning content around them, products, even. Then I read the terms, and I felt that tiny bit of discouragement you feel when something free turns out to have a fence around it.

What the terms actually say

I checked Meta’s AI Terms of Service on October 18, 2026, the terms Meta’s own documentation points to. They give you ownership of your prompts, not your outputs. The voices stay Meta’s property. The terms don’t ban commercial use outright, but they don’t grant it either, and every bit of responsibility for how you use the voices sits with you.

I’m not telling you what you can’t do. I’m telling you to be careful, because the facts say this: don’t build anything you’d need to defend in a dispute. The platforms agree, in their own way. YouTube asks creators to disclose synthetic content, and Meta asks for labels on realistic-sounding AI audio. The free voices are for exploring. Anything you publish or monetize should run through a voice you actually hold the rights to.

The $6 line

That feeling? That’s what the $6 line buys.

Explore all you want, audition voices as scratch tracks, use short clips as examples when you’re writing about the tools. But anything you publish or monetize should run through a voice you actually hold the rights to. That’s the $6 line: ElevenLabs Starter is where your voice becomes yours, with the commercial license to prove it.

What the $6 gets you: voice cloning from a short recording of yourself, so the voice is actually yours. A commercial license, so you can publish and monetize whatever you make with it. And directed delivery means you can steer tone with inline tags, the way a director steers an actor, instead of taking whatever the voice gives you.

How the swap works

Here’s the workflow that makes the free-to-paid jump painless. Build everything against a scratch track, a rough placeholder recording that holds your timing while you edit. The script is the part that transfers: same words, pasted into ElevenLabs, generated in your real voice. What doesn’t transfer is the timing, because every voice speaks at its own pace, so you nudge your clips to land on the new pauses.

Don’t lock your cuts too tightly to the scratch track. Leave room to slide things when the real voice lands, and the swap takes minutes instead of hours.

Who this is for

Anyone making content with AI voices who plans to publish it: videos, courses, commercials, anything with an audience. If it’s just for you, the free voices are plenty. The moment money or the public enters the picture, that’s when the license matters.

Are you building something right now that a voice will carry? Then read the terms of every AI tool in it. Future you says thanks.
